html:
The sweet potato, a plant domesticated in the Americas, was growing in eastern Polynesia by about 1000 CE, centuries before Columbus. Charred sweet potato remains in the Cook Islands date to around then. It is the strongest clue that Polynesians and South Americans met before Europeans reached either.

Polynesian sailors were then settling the far east of the Pacific; see Settlement of East Polynesia. Most scholars think some of them reached the coast of South America and came back with the plant. A Polynesian word for it, kumala or kūmara, resembles a word used in the Andes. A 2020 genetic study found Native American ancestry in some eastern Polynesian peoples dating to around 1200, which supports contact. A few botanists argue the seeds might have drifted across the ocean on their own.

The sweet potato became a staple across Polynesia, and in New Zealand it was one of the few tropical crops that could grow in the cool south; see Māori settle Aotearoa. Europeans later carried it to Asia separately; see Sweet potato reaches China.
